text: This is the job-ready capstone: one real deployment project, built across four lessons, pulling together every chapter of this course. The company is Harrow Peak Outfitters, a 35-person outdoor-gear retailer whose order-processing app and database have run for six years on one aging physical server with no redundancy and manual USB backups. You're the engineer who owns moving it to the cloud, end to end.

Before opening any portal, you write down what the business actually needs, with Operations Manager Dana Oyelaran. The app has to be reachable 6 AM to 10 PM Pacific. Customer order data must stay in the US. The budget is modest and there's no 24/7 ops team -- just you -- so every piece added has to earn its complexity. None of that is a technical decision yet; it's the constraint every technical decision has to satisfy.

Harrow Peak already runs Microsoft 365 and Entra ID, and you're already Azure-trained -- running a second cloud would add overhead this project doesn't need. For sizing, you pull real CPU and memory numbers off the old server for the past month instead of guessing, which lands on a Standard_D2s_v5 app VM: enough headroom for the real peak, not padded for an imaginary one.

One VNet, three subnets, each with one job: app-subnet for the order VM, data-subnet for the database's private endpoint, mgmt-subnet for admin access only. Network deploys before any compute or storage, in order, and every NSG is scoped to exactly what its subnet needs from the first rule -- RDP allowed only from Harrow Peak's one static office IP, the database reachable only from app-subnet, nothing opened wide and tightened later.

Before moving on, you verify a test host in app-subnet can actually reach the database's private endpoint -- confirming the network works before anything depends on it. Next: deploying compute and storage into this network, and wiring them together with a managed identity instead of a hardcoded key.
